source.title: Study of the double trigger phenomenon and comparison of minimax approximation with L2-regularization

record.file_problem: none; the full paper is present, although the extracted text does not include the plotted data values.
record.tranche_reason: It sweeps polynomial degree and measures test error to study double descent, but uses polynomial regression rather than the original deep-network setting and reports no direct reproduction of the original method.
record.gate_note: The study reports test MSE against polynomial degree for unregularized, L2-regularized, and minimax polynomial regression, including conditions with different outlier and noise levels. Results stated only as plot values are recorded as figure-only. It does not vary epochs or training-set size. References to prior work are not recorded as findings.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps polynomial degree past the 70-point training-set size with an unregularized pseudo-inverse fit and reports test MSE. This is a non-deep model class with a direct result on whether a second descent appears (V4). It is a new setting, not a reproduction of either original.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say that without regularization, double descent did not fully appear: error rose, with short local dips, likely due to outliers. They conclude L2 is more stable at high degrees and under heavy noise or outliers, while minimax is better at low degrees (up to 50) with few anomalies.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses synthetic sinusoidal data, polynomial regression, degree sweeps, and test MSE, with outlier and noise variations; it does not reproduce the original deep-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with polynomial degree, outlier fraction, noise level, and regression method.

fits_no_version.finding: Ridge (unstated alpha) shows stable, gradually increasing test MSE across degrees, while minimax fits degrade with more outliers and noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Choice of fitting method or regularizer controls high-degree error growth in outlier-contaminated polynomial regression.

record.problems: The supplied text gives no numeric test-error values for the plotted results, no uncertainty estimates or repetitions, and does not state the maximum polynomial degree or the Ridge regularization parameter. The data are synthetic and the described main experiment uses 70 training points. The figures are not available as readable plotted data in the supplied text.

untested.parts: Deep networks; only polynomial regression is used.
Epoch-wise curves; models are closed-form or convex fits.
Model classes other than polynomial regression; clean data without outliers; unregularized fits at other noise or outlier levels.
No unregularized curves across noise levels; no tuned regularization; no multiple peaks examined.

missing.what: Table of MSE reductions for the methods (Appendix 1), referenced in the text but not supplied
Maximum degree, Ridge alpha, and test-set size are not stated; the location of the interpolation threshold relative to the curve cannot be checked

record.verdict_notes: The record's label of Ridge rows as V4 evidence is removed, because Ridge is non-interpolating and its curves are method comparisons. The single V4 verdict rests on a qualitative description of one curve. It comes from one synthetic run with heavy outliers, no repetitions, and a normal-equations formula written for an overparameterized fit, which may be numerically ill-conditioned. Weight the challenge accordingly. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network model-wise double descent; the tested models are polynomial regressions.
Changing training sample size near an interpolation threshold.
Other model classes beyond the tested polynomial regressions; no explicit interpolation-threshold measurement.
No single effective-complexity measure is used to predict peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.

The study varies noise and regularization but does not test whether a double-descent peak is caused by label noise or variance, whether peaks split, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes a peak.
No alternative effective-parameter count or test of whether that count turns a second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

relationships.condition: Unregularized pseudo-inverse polynomial regression, 70 training points, 40% large outliers, degrees past 70 up to 200+
relationships.reason: R1: the text says error is predominantly increasing, with no substantial decline at high degrees, and that double descent does not fully manifest. This is qualitative only, from a single synthetic setting.
relationships.display_finding: With 70 training points and 40% large outliers, error predominantly increased through degrees above 200 without substantial high-degree recovery in the single synthetic setting.
